title: Combined effects of acoustic, thermal, and illumination conditions on the comfort of discrete senses and overall indoor environment
research_question: To investigate the influence of multisensory interaction on acoustic comfort, thermal comfort, visual comfort, and indoor environmental comfort with three physical indoor environmental factors (acoustic, thermal, and illumination conditions) in an environmentally controlled laboratory.

participants.description: 60 university students (30 men, 30 women) from South Korea. Women: Mean age 21.3 (S.D 1.7) years, mean height 162.4 (S.D 5.7) cm, mean weight 55.7 (S.D 8.3) kg. Men: Mean age 23.27 (S.D 1.6) years, mean height 175.5 (S.D 5.4) cm, mean weight 69.5 (S.D 7.4) kg. All had normal hearing (0-25 dB HL) and normal or corrected-to-normal vision, with no color deficiency. Participants wore a clothing ensemble of approximately 0.75 clo.
participants.recruitment: Received financial support for their participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four different sound sources (babble, fan, music, water) played at four sound levels (45, 55, 65, 75 dBA). Ambient noise (35 dBA) was also included as a reference case.
Three homogenous room temperatures (20, 25, and 30 °C) with a constant relative humidity of 45%.
Three illuminance levels on the participants' desk surface (150, 500, and 1000 lx).

mechanisms: Humans perceive environments through the interaction and integration among various sensory stimuli.
Multisensory interaction influences perception of comfort.
implementation_implications: Effects of gender should be considered in the range of physical conditions.
Gender difference cannot be generalized without consideration of the environmental conditions.

limitations: The experimental design might have allowed participants to focus on acoustic variations rather than on thermal or illumination conditions, potentially limiting generalizability.
Illuminance was the sole physical factor for visual comfort in this study; other visual factors such as color temperature, wall color, and window views were not investigated.
Gender differences cannot be generalized without consideration of the specific environmental conditions tested.

paper_metadata.title: Making imagination even more embodied: imagination, constraint and epistemic relevance
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Making imagination even more embodied: imagination, constraint and epistemic relevance
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThis paper considers the epistemic role that embodiment plays in imagining. We focus on two aspects of embodied cognition understood in its strong sense: explicit motoric processes related to performance, and neuronal processes rooted in bodily and action processes, and describe their role in imagining. The paper argues that these two aspects of strongly embodied cognition can play distinctive and positive roles in constraining imagining, thereby complementing Amy Kind's argument for the epistemic relevance of imagination "under constraints" and Magdalena Balcerak Jackson's argument for justification by imagination.
